unit.title: Flags, safety cars and who is in charge
unit.summary: Flags, neutralisations, stewards and the penalty menu.

lessons.title: The flags you will see
lessons.objective: Recognise yellow, red, blue, black and chequered and what each demands.

payload.prompt: What does this yellow flag mean?

options.text: Danger ahead; slow down and no overtaking in that sector.
The session is being paused and all cars return to the pits.
Lapped drivers must let the faster car through.
The race has finished and drivers are crossing the line.

cues: Yellow = caution, not a full stop.
Track ahead has debris or a slow car.

explanation.correct: Right. Yellow flags signal danger: crash, debris, or weather. Drivers must slow down and cannot pass in that marshalling sector.
explanation.incorrect: Yellow is a caution: there is danger ahead, so slow down and do not overtake in that sector until the all-clear.
explanation.sayThisLine: Yellow flag in sector two, so he had to lift.

payload.prompt: What does this red flag mean?

options.text: Stop immediately: the session is suspended and cars return to pits.
Slow down because there is a hazard on the track.
You are disqualified from the race.
You must serve a time penalty for a rule breach.

cues: Red = full stop; the entire session halts.
Used after big crashes or unsafe conditions.

explanation.correct: Right. A red flag stops the entire session. All drivers must slow down, return to the pits and the race will restart.
explanation.incorrect: Red is the harshest flag: it stops the session completely, not just a sector. Yellow is caution; red is stop.
explanation.sayThisLine: Red flag, the whole session stopped.

payload.prompt: What does this blue flag mean?

options.text: You are lapped: let the faster car through, or face a penalty.
You have been disqualified from the race.
There is danger on the track and you must slow down.
The race has finished and it is safe to slow down.

cues: Blue = 'out of the way': you are lapped.
A faster driver is about to pass you.

explanation.correct: Right. A blue flag tells a lapped driver to yield to the car behind. Ignoring it can earn a penalty.
explanation.incorrect: Blue flags are for lapped traffic only: the faster car is about to lap you, so let it through.
explanation.sayThisLine: He ignored the blue flags and got a penalty.

payload.prompt: What does this black flag mean?

options.text: You are disqualified from the race and must return to pits immediately.
You have a time penalty to serve.
You are lapped and must let the leader through.
The session is paused due to dangerous weather.

cues: The harshest flag a driver can receive.

explanation.correct: Right. The black flag is the harshest penalty: immediate disqualification from the race. The driver must return to the pits.
explanation.incorrect: Black is disqualification, the harshest flag. A black-and-white flag is a warning; black alone means you are out.
explanation.sayThisLine: The black flag, he is disqualified.

payload.prompt: Match each flag to what it signals.

pairs.definition: Marks the end of the race for each driver as they cross the finish line.
Signals danger ahead; drivers must slow and cannot pass in that sector.
Stops the entire session; all cars must return to the pits and the race will restart.
Tells a lapped driver to let the faster car through; ignoring it earns a penalty.

distractorDefinitions: You are disqualified from the race.
You have a time penalty to serve.

explanation.summary: Flags communicate the race status: yellow = caution, red = stop, blue = yield, chequered = finish.
explanation.sayThisLine: The flags tell you what is happening on the track.

payload.prompt: What does a double yellow flag mean?

options.text: Danger on track; be ready to stop and do not overtake.
options.explanation: A double yellow means caution is even more serious: there may be a car stopped or debris and you must be prepared to stop suddenly.

options.text: The session is over and drivers can cool down.
options.explanation: That is the end of the race, not a double yellow. Double yellow is a heightened caution.

options.text: Two drivers have been given penalties.
options.explanation: Flags do not track penalties, they signal track conditions. Double yellow is a serious caution.

options.text: The entire session is suspended and will restart on the grid.
options.explanation: That is a red flag. Double yellow is a serious caution in a sector, not a full stop.

explanation.correct: Right. Double yellow is a heightened caution: there is a serious hazard and you must be ready to stop. The incident is worse than a single yellow.
explanation.incorrect: Double yellow means heightened danger: be ready to stop. It is not as severe as red (full stop), but more serious than a single yellow caution.
explanation.sayThisLine: Double yellow down the straight, he had to be ready to stop.

payload.prompt: How does a black-and-white flag differ from a solid black flag?

options.text: Black-and-white warns of unsportsmanlike conduct; black means disqualification.
options.explanation: Correct. Black-and-white = warning; black = you are out. Both relate to conduct, not track conditions.

options.text: They mean the same thing: the driver is disqualified.
options.explanation: No. Black-and-white is a warning; solid black is disqualification. The distinction matters.

options.text: Black-and-white is for crashes; black is for unsportsmanlike driving.
options.explanation: It is the opposite. Black-and-white warns of unsportsmanlike conduct; black is the final dismissal.

options.text: Black-and-white means session ending; black means it is being paused.
options.explanation: Neither is about session status. Black flags relate to driver conduct and penalty stages.

explanation.correct: Right. A black-and-white flag is a warning for unsportsmanlike driving. If it continues, the black flag comes next and the driver is out.
explanation.incorrect: The black-and-white flag warns a driver to stop unsportsmanlike behaviour. If it continues, the black flag comes next and the driver is disqualified.
explanation.sayThisLine: That got a black-and-white flag, a warning to clean it up.

lessons.title: Why the safety car exists
lessons.objective: Explain what a safety car does to the gaps and to the race.

payload.prompt: What does a safety car do to the gaps between cars?

options.text: It bunches the pack by slowing everyone to the same speed, erasing gaps.
options.explanation: Right. The safety car brings all drivers down to a controlled speed, which closes the gaps that were opened during the race.

options.text: It keeps the gaps the same by pacing all cars evenly.
options.explanation: That is what the Virtual Safety Car does. The physical safety car bunches the pack.

options.text: It increases the gaps because faster cars have to slow more.
options.explanation: No. The safety car slows the leader the same as the backmarkers. Everyone bunches.

options.text: It removes the fastest car from the race temporarily.
options.explanation: The safety car is just a pace car; it does not remove anyone. It brings the field together.

explanation.correct: Right. A safety car bunches the field by leading them at reduced speed. If a driver was leading by ten seconds, the bunching erases that gap.
explanation.incorrect: The safety car paces all drivers at the same speed, so gaps close. Everyone goes slow; no one is ahead. It is a reset button.
explanation.sayThisLine: The safety car ruined his ten-second lead.

payload.prompt: When does the race director deploy the safety car?

options.text: After a crash, debris, medical emergency or dangerous track conditions.
options.explanation: Right. The safety car is used to neutralise the race and protect marshals and medical staff.

options.text: Whenever a driver falls more than five seconds behind.
options.explanation: That is not the safety car's job. The safety car is for track safety, not position.

options.text: Every time a driver pits for tyres.
options.explanation: No. Pit stops happen during normal racing; the safety car is only for serious incidents.

options.text: At the request of the leading team.
options.explanation: The race director makes the call independently for safety reasons, not on team request.

explanation.correct: Right. The race director is the FIA official who decides when to deploy the safety car. It is always for safety: crash, debris, medical response.
explanation.incorrect: The safety car is a protective tool, not a strategy aid. It comes out for track safety: crashes, debris, medical emergencies.
explanation.sayThisLine: The race director called the safety car because of the debris.

payload.prompt: A driver is leading by eight seconds when the safety car comes out. What happens next?

options.text: The safety car closes the gap and the field bunches behind the leader.
options.explanation: Right. The safety car brings everyone to the same speed, so the eight-second gap closes to just car lengths.

options.text: The leader maintains the eight-second gap because they are ahead of the safety car.
options.explanation: No. The safety car is the pace car; the leader follows behind it at the slow speed, so the gap closes.

options.text: The gap increases because the leader can drive faster than the safety car.
options.explanation: The safety car sets a fixed pace and the leader cannot break away. Everyone follows at the same speed.

options.text: The race ends immediately and the leader wins.
options.explanation: The safety car does not end the race; it pauses the action and the race restarts.

explanation.correct: Right. When the safety car comes out, the leading driver is caught and the field bunches behind the pace car. The lead is lost until the restart.
explanation.incorrect: The safety car leads all drivers at a slow pace, so gaps close. A ten-second lead becomes a few car lengths.
explanation.sayThisLine: The safety car bunched the field right up.

payload.prompt: Can drivers pass each other behind the safety car?

scene.alt: Two cars following the safety car at reduced pace; the second car is beside the first but both are behind the pace car.

explanation.correct: Right. When the safety car is out, passing is forbidden. All drivers must stay in order and follow the pace car.
explanation.incorrect: No passing under the safety car. The race is paused at the safety car speed, and no overtaking is allowed until the restart.
explanation.sayThisLine: No passing under the safety car.

payload.prompt: A car is on fire at the barrier. Does the race director use the safety car?

scene.alt: A car burning at the side of the track with marshals and medical crews responding.

explanation.correct: Right. A fire and marshals on track means the session must be stopped completely. A red flag brings all cars back to the pits.
explanation.incorrect: A fire is too dangerous for the safety car pace. This requires a red flag to stop the entire session and bring all cars to the pits.

lessons.title: VSC or full safety car?
lessons.objective: Tell the two apart and say which suits which incident.

payload.prompt: Does VSC preserve gaps while safety car bunches?

scene.alt: Gap comparison: VSC shows two cars with the same gap after the safety protocol; full safety car shows two cars very close after bunching.

explanation.correct: Right. The Virtual Safety Car (VSC) slows everyone by the same delta time, so gaps stay. The physical safety car bunches the field.
explanation.incorrect: That is the key difference: VSC preserves gaps (everyone slows the same amount), physical safety car closes gaps (bunching).

payload.prompt: Debris is far from the racing line. Is VSC appropriate?

scene.alt: A piece of debris at the side of the track, away from the main racing path.

explanation.correct: Right. Debris far from the line does not require a physical safety car. A VSC is safer and lets the race continue with gaps intact.
explanation.incorrect: Debris off the line can be handled with VSC: just slow everything down, then resume. Only crash and debris on the line need a full safety car.

payload.prompt: A car is stalled mid-track and marshals are going out. Is a full safety car required?

scene.alt: A car stopped in the centre of the track with marshals running out to aid it.

explanation.correct: Right. Marshals out on track need the full safety car so all drivers slow and bunch safely. A VSC does not bring drivers close enough to avoid hitting marshals.
explanation.incorrect: When marshals or medical staff are on the track, a full safety car is needed to slow the field properly and protect them.

payload.prompt: What safety action for a mid-track collision?

facts.label: Incident
facts.value: Two cars have collided mid-track; both off-line.

facts.label: Marshals
facts.value: No marshals on track; drivers can reach the pits.

facts.label: Debris
facts.value: Small debris clears in minutes, not on racing line.

options.label: Virtual Safety Car
options.consequence: The field slows by a set delta but gaps stay the same. The cars clear the track and debris is cleaned, then the race resumes.
considerations: Both drivers are safe and no marshals are at risk.
Gaps are preserved, which is fair to drivers with a lead.

options.label: Full Safety Car
options.consequence: The field bunches and the race resets. Drivers pit if needed, then a restart happens.
considerations: Safer option with two damaged cars and debris cleanup needed.

payload.expertNote: Race directors prefer full safety car for on-track collisions with debris; VSC for off-line minor incidents where no one is at risk.
payload.sayThisLine: Full safety car for the debris on the track.

payload.prompt: Why choose VSC instead of full safety car?

options.text: To slow the field and preserve gaps so the race stays fair.
options.explanation: Right. VSC is used when safety is needed but fairness matters too: gaps stay the same, so the leading car is not punished.

options.text: To bunch the field and reset the race completely.
options.explanation: That is what the full safety car does, not VSC. VSC keeps gaps.

options.text: To allow overtaking while the race is paused.
options.explanation: No. Overtaking is not allowed under VSC or safety car. Both are safety pauses.

options.text: To end the race immediately without a restart.
options.explanation: Neither VSC nor safety car ends the race. Both pause and restart it.

explanation.correct: Right. The VSC balances safety and fairness: the field slows, but gaps are preserved so the leader's advantage is not erased.
explanation.incorrect: VSC keeps gaps, so it is fair to drivers who built a lead. Full safety car bunches and resets, used for bigger incidents.
explanation.sayThisLine: VSC so the gaps stay the same.

lessons.title: Red flags and restarts
lessons.objective: Explain what a red flag allows and how the race restarts.

payload.prompt: What is the order after a red flag?

items.text: All drivers slow down and return to the pits under caution.
items.why: The red flag stops the race and brings everyone back safely.

items.text: Cars are parked in parc ferme and major set-up changes are not allowed.
items.why: Parc ferme locks down the cars for fairness and safety.

items.text: Drivers may change tyres and make repairs, as allowed by the rules.
items.why: Tyres and repairs are permitted; big aerodynamic changes are not.

items.text: The drivers line up on the grid in their current positions and the race restarts.
items.why: A standing restart is a fresh lights-out start from the grid.

explanation.correct: Right. Red flag: all stop, enter parc ferme, minimal changes allowed, restart on grid.
explanation.incorrect: Red flag stops the race, brings cars back, limits set-up changes, and restarts from the grid with lights-out.

payload.prompt: What is the purpose of a red flag?

options.text: To stop the entire session and bring cars back to the pits for safety.
options.explanation: Right. Red flags stop the race when there is too much debris, a big crash, or dangerous conditions.

options.text: To disqualify the leading driver from the race.
options.explanation: That is not the purpose of a red flag. Red flags are about safety, not penalties.

options.text: To warn drivers to slow down in one sector.
options.explanation: That is a yellow flag. Red is a full stop, not a warning in one area.

options.text: To signal the end of qualifying so drivers can cool down.
options.explanation: Red flags pause the race due to safety, not to signal the end of a session.

explanation.correct: Right. A red flag is the most serious track signal: the session is stopped completely, usually because of a major crash, large debris or dangerous conditions.
explanation.incorrect: Red flags are for safety: a big crash, debris everywhere, dangerous weather or marshals in peril. The entire session stops.
explanation.sayThisLine: Red flag, the whole session stopped.

payload.prompt: What is parc ferme and what happens after a red flag?

options.text: A secure area where cars are parked and major set-up changes are not allowed.
options.explanation: Right. Parc ferme means cars are locked down. Teams can change tyres and make repairs, but not big aerodynamic or suspension changes.

options.text: A penalty zone where drivers wait if they broke a rule.
options.explanation: Parc ferme is not a penalty area. It is a technical lock-down area for car security.

options.text: A free pit area where teams can make any changes they want.
options.explanation: No. Parc ferme is the opposite: it restricts what teams can change. It is a seal on the car.

options.text: A zone where damaged cars are destroyed after crashing.
options.explanation: Parc ferme is for car security and technical regulation, not destruction.

explanation.correct: Right. Parc ferme is a rules lock-down: cars are parked and teams cannot make major changes. Tyres yes, engine settings yes, wing angle no.
explanation.incorrect: Parc ferme means 'closed park': the car is locked down to a basic spec. Teams cannot change wings, springs or set-up, only tyres and repairs.
explanation.sayThisLine: Once parc ferme is on, no more big changes.

payload.prompt: How does the race restart after a red flag?

options.text: Drivers line up on the grid in their running order and the lights go out.
options.explanation: Right. A standing restart is like a race start: cars are on the grid in their positions and the lights go out.

options.text: Drivers immediately resume racing from the pits at half-speed.
options.explanation: No. A standing restart is a full stop on the grid with a fresh lights-out start.

options.text: The safety car leads the field back onto track and then leaves.
options.explanation: After a red flag, a standing restart is clean: drivers go from the grid with lights-out, no safety car lead.

options.text: The race is declared over and the highest-placed driver at the time of the red flag wins.
options.explanation: A red flag does not end the race. It pauses and restarts it. The race continues after the restart.

explanation.correct: Right. A standing restart is a full restart: cars line up on the grid, lights go out, and they race off again.
explanation.incorrect: After a red flag, the race restarts from the grid with a fresh lights-out start. It is a complete reset.
explanation.sayThisLine: After the red flag they had a standing restart.

lessons.title: Stewards and the penalty menu
lessons.objective: Match common infringements to typical penalties.

payload.prompt: Match each penalty type to its effect.

pairs.definition: Seconds added to a driver's race time after the race ends, usually 5 or 10 seconds.
Positions dropped on the starting grid at the next race for technical breaches.
Licence points for dangerous driving; 12 within 12 months means a one-race ban.
FIA officials who investigate on-track incidents and hand out penalties.

distractorDefinitions: A monetary fine paid to the FIA.

explanation.summary: Stewards investigate, then issue time penalties (added to race time), grid penalties (starting position drop) or penalty points (licence points).
explanation.sayThisLine: The stewards gave him a five-second penalty for that.

payload.prompt: Match each driving breach to its typical penalty.

pairs.definition: Leaving pit box into another car's path or with unsecured wheel. Typically earns a time penalty.
Hitting another driver through aggressive or careless driving. Typically earns a time penalty.
Taking more than the allocated power-unit elements. Earns a grid penalty at the next race.

distractorDefinitions: Crossing track limits and gaining an advantage.
Ignoring a blue flag during the race.

explanation.summary: On-track infractions (unsafe release, contact) earn time penalties; technical breaches (extra parts) earn grid penalties.
explanation.sayThisLine: That was an unsafe release from the pits.

payload.prompt: What is the stewards' job in F1?

options.text: Investigate incidents during the race and hand out penalties to drivers.
options.explanation: Right. The stewards are independent FIA officials who review on-track contact and rule breaches, then decide penalties.

options.text: Control the start, the safety car and the red flags.
options.explanation: That is the race director's job. Stewards handle incidents; the race director handles the session flow.

options.text: Operate the timing system and display the results on screen.
options.explanation: That is the FIA timing team, not the stewards. Stewards are judges.

options.text: Check that teams follow the technical regulations on the cars.
options.explanation: That is technical officials at the race, not the stewards. Stewards focus on driving conduct.

explanation.correct: Right. Stewards are judges: they review incidents, watch video, hear driver statements and decide on penalties.
explanation.incorrect: Stewards are the judges of racing conduct. They investigate contact, rule breaches and unsportsmanlike behaviour, then hand down penalties.
explanation.sayThisLine: The stewards gave him a penalty for that.

payload.prompt: What happens if a driver gets 12 penalty points within 12 months?

options.text: The driver receives a one-race ban.
options.explanation: Right. Twelve penalty points in a rolling 12-month window means the driver is suspended for one race.

options.text: The driver is fined money by the FIA.
options.explanation: Fines and points are different. Twelve points = ban, not a fine.

options.text: The driver's team is given a constructors' penalty.
options.explanation: Penalty points are on the driver's licence, not the team. The ban is individual.

options.text: The driver loses five grid positions at the next race.
options.explanation: That is a grid penalty. Twelve penalty points = a one-race ban, which is harsher.

explanation.correct: Right. Penalty points accumulate on a driver's super licence. Twelve points within 12 months trigger an automatic one-race ban.
explanation.incorrect: Twelve penalty points in 12 months = one-race ban. It is the harshest driver penalty short of a permanent suspension.
explanation.sayThisLine: He is on eight penalty points now.

payload.prompt: How is a time penalty served in F1?

options.text: The driver's crew holds the car for penalty seconds, or it is added to the final race time.
options.explanation: Right. A time penalty is either served in the pits (crew holds the car longer) or added after the race ends.

options.text: The driver must sit still on track for the penalty seconds.
options.explanation: No. Time penalties are served in the pits or added to the final time, not sitting on track.

options.text: The driver's lap times are multiplied by the penalty seconds.
options.explanation: Time penalties are fixed seconds added once, not multiplied to all laps.

options.text: The driver is dropped positions on the grid at the next race.
options.explanation: That is a grid penalty. A time penalty is five seconds added to the race time.

explanation.correct: Right. A time penalty can be served in the pits (crew holds the car for five seconds, costing lap time) or added to the final race time after the chequered flag.
explanation.incorrect: Five-second time penalties are served by the pit crew or added to the final time. They change the result, not the grid position.

payload.sayThisLine: A five-second penalty for that move.

payload.prompt: What penalty for a braking-zone contact?

facts.label: Incident
facts.value: Two drivers made contact in a braking zone; the second car hit the rear wing.

facts.label: Result
facts.value: The first car was knocked off line but recovered and finished the race.

facts.label: Video
facts.value: The second driver was late turning in; appears deliberate but aggressive.

options.label: Five-second penalty
options.consequence: The aggressive but not destructive contact is punished lightly; the driver keeps their position but loses time in the penalty addition.
considerations: Proportional: the driver caused contact but did not take the other car out.

options.label: Ten-second penalty
options.consequence: A harsher penalty for deliberate or very reckless contact; the driver may even lose their position.
considerations: Appropriate if the stewards judge it deliberate or dangerous.

payload.expertNote: Stewards weigh whether contact was accidental (light penalty), careless (five seconds) or deliberate and dangerous (ten seconds or more).

lessons.title: Track limits and unsafe releases
lessons.objective: Apply track limits and pit-release rules to simple cases.

payload.prompt: Do all four wheels over the track limit delete the lap?

scene.alt: Bird's-eye view of a corner: white kerb line at the edge, a car's track shown with all four wheels outside the line.

explanation.correct: Right. If all four wheels go over the limit and the driver gains an advantage (faster corner), the lap is deleted and does not count.
explanation.incorrect: Track limits are enforced with a video check: if all four wheels are over the line and advantage is gained, the lap is invalid.

payload.prompt: Is a car released from the pits with one loose wheel nut an unsafe release?

scene.alt: Pit box view: a car being released with a wheel nut visibly loose on one corner.

explanation.correct: Right. An unsafe release is when a car leaves the pit box with a wheel not secure, or into the path of another car.
explanation.incorrect: A loose wheel is definitely unsafe. The pit crew must secure all wheels before release.

payload.prompt: If a lapped driver slows to let a faster car pass the blue flag, is this correct?

scene.alt: Two cars on track: the rear car displaying a blue flag, the front car (lapped) appearing to slow deliberately.

explanation.correct: Right. A lapped driver must let the faster car through when given a blue flag. Deliberately slowing or blocking earns a penalty.
explanation.incorrect: Blue flags demand obedience. The lapped driver must yield. Slow down, let the faster car pass, follow their line.

payload.prompt: In a race, a driver runs over the track limit line but stays on track and does not gain lap time. Is a penalty applied?

options.text: No penalty, because no advantage was gained.
options.explanation: Right. Track limits are only enforced if the driver gains an advantage. Running over the line but not getting faster means no penalty.

options.text: Yes, a penalty applies automatically for any wheels over the line.
options.explanation: No. Track limits are about advantage gained, not just being over the line. Stewards use data to check lap times.

options.text: It depends on how many times the driver has run over the line.
options.explanation: Repeated violations might be noted, but the key is whether an advantage was gained on that lap.

options.text: The driver is disqualified from the race.
options.explanation: Track-limit breaches are minor infractions. Disqualification is for serious rule breaches, not track limits.

explanation.correct: Right. Track-limit enforcement is about advantage: if all four wheels are over and the lap time is faster, it is deleted. No advantage = no penalty.
explanation.incorrect: Track limits are policed by data: stewards check if an advantage was gained. Running wide without gaining time is not penalised.

payload.sayThisLine: Track limits deleted his best lap.

payload.prompt: A car is released from the pit box and collides with an oncoming car in the pit lane. What penalty?

options.text: An unsafe-release penalty (usually five seconds) for leaving into the path of another car.
options.explanation: Right. The pit crew is responsible for releasing safely. If another car is coming, the crew must hold the car.

options.text: No penalty, because the collision was not the driver's fault.
options.explanation: The crew and driver are responsible for the release. An unsafe release earns a penalty.

options.text: Both cars are penalised equally for being in the pit lane together.
options.explanation: The released car is penalised for the unsafe release. The oncoming car may also get a penalty depending on circumstances.

options.text: The team is disqualified from the race.
options.explanation: A single unsafe release is a time penalty, not disqualification.

explanation.correct: Right. An unsafe release is a pit-lane infraction: the crew did not clear the way before releasing. It earns a time penalty.
explanation.incorrect: Unsafe releases (into other cars or with unsecured wheels) are penalised. The pit crew's job is to ensure safety.

payload.sayThisLine: An unsafe release from the pits.
